questions.prompt: For a controller \(C\) in series with a plant \(P\), and with the output subtracted from the reference, the loop transfer function is
questions.explanation: One trip around the loop meets \(C\) and then \(P\), so \(L\) is the product \(PC\). The sum \(P+C\) is not that trip. Either ratio leaves one of the two blocks inverted.

questions.prompt: A plant has gain \(P=3\) and the controller has gain \(C=5\). What is the loop gain \(L=PC\)?
questions.explanation: The product is \(3 \times 5 = 15\). The sum \(8\) skips the series connection, and \(5/3\) is the controller over the plant.

questions.prompt: Write the loop transfer function of a series controller and plant, using the names \(P\) and \(C\).
questions.explanation: The loop transfer function is the product \(PC\). The sum \(P+C\) is a parallel connection. The ratio \(P/C\) inverts the controller.

questions.prompt: A plant \(P=4\) is under a controller \(C=2\), with the output subtracted from the reference. An input disturbance, added at the plant input, reaches the output through \(P/(1+PC)\). What is that gain?
questions.explanation: The loop gain is \(PC=8\), so the input-disturbance map is \(4/(1+8)=4/9\). The sensitivity \(1/(1+8)\) leaves out the plant. The plant gain \(4\) is the open-loop path, before the loop is closed.

questions.prompt: Sensor noise is subtracted with the measured output. Which of the four maps multiplies that noise into the output?
questions.explanation: Noise that enters with the measurement is rejected from the output only when \(T\) is small. The output sees that noise through \(T\). \(S\) multiplies an output disturbance, \(PS\) multiplies a plant-input disturbance, and \(CS\) builds the command from the reference.

questions.prompt: Order the construction of the four closed-loop maps from a plant \(P\) and a controller \(C\).
questions.explanation: The four maps \(S\), \(T\), \(PS\), and \(CS\) share the denominator \(1+PC\). The product \(L\) has to exist before that denominator does, and the denominator has to exist before the four divisions. Dividing by \(L\) alone drops the return difference.

questions.prompt: A note builds the map from a plant-input disturbance to the output. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The sensitivity multiplies a disturbance that is already at the output. A disturbance at the plant input still has to pass through \(P\), so the map is \(P/(1+L)\). The loop product and the return difference in the first steps are right.

questions.prompt: A controller \(C=6\) drives a plant \(P=0.5\). The map from reference to the command \(u\) is \(C/(1+PC)\). What is that gain?
questions.explanation: The loop gain is \(PC=3\), so \(C/(1+PC)=6/4=1.5\). The complementary sensitivity \(3/4\) is the reference-to-output map, not the command map. The controller gain \(6\) is the command only when the error is \(1\) and the loop is open.

questions.explanation: \(S\), \(T\), and \(CS\) are three of the four closed-loop maps, and each divides by \(1+PC\). The sum \(P+C\) is not one of those maps and has no return difference in it.

questions.prompt: Preview of a Nyquist plot. At DC the plant gain is \(8\) and the controller gain is \(1.5\). What is the DC loop gain the plot starts from?
questions.explanation: The DC loop gain is \(PC=8 \times 1.5 = 12\). A Nyquist plot of \(L\) starts at that real value when the frequency is zero. The sum \(9.5\) is not \(L(0)\), and \(8/1.5\) divides the plant by the controller.

questions.prompt: Preview of disturbance and tracking readings. An output disturbance reaches the output through which map?
questions.explanation: An output disturbance is multiplied by \(S\) on its way to the output. A later skill uses that fact to measure attenuation, noise, and tracking error. \(T\) multiplies the reference and the sensor noise. \(CS\) builds the command. \(L\) is the loop, not a closed-loop map.

questions.prompt: Preview of the root locus. A plant \(P=2\) is under a controller \(C=3\). What is the return difference \(1+PC\)?
questions.explanation: The loop gain is \(6\), so the return difference is \(1+6=7\). Closed-loop poles are the roots of that difference set to zero, which a later skill traces as gain changes. The loop gain \(6\) is one less than the return difference.

retired_questions.prompt: The loop transfer function \(L(s)\) is the product of
retired_questions.explanation: Walk from the error, through the forward path, through the return path, back to the summing junction. Multiply every block you pass. That product is \(L(s)\). The reference and output are signals, not gains. The closed-loop gain times sensitivity equals \(T \cdot S = L/(1+L)^2\), which is not \(L\). The numerator and denominator of the plant describe only the forward block.

retired_questions.prompt: A unity-feedback loop has forward gain \(G = 6\). The loop gain is
retired_questions.explanation: Unity feedback means \(H = 1\), so \(L = G \times 1 = 6\). The closed-loop gain \(6/7\) is not the loop gain. Subtracting 1 from 6 gives 5, which is not defined by the diagram.

retired_questions.explanation: \(L = 8 \times 0.5 = 4\), so \(1 + L = 5\). The loop gain 4 is one less than the return difference. The closed-loop gain \(8/5\) is not the return difference.

retired_questions.explanation: At \(s = 0\), the loop gain is \(L(0) = 12 \times 1 = 12\). The closed-loop gain \(12/13\) is what the reference sees. The sensitivity \(1/13\) is the disturbance attenuation.

retired_questions.prompt: For sensitivity analysis: forward gain 5, return gain 0.4. The sensitivity \(S\) is
retired_questions.explanation: \(L = 2\), so \(S = 1/3 = 0.333\). The complementary sensitivity \(2/3\) is what the reference sees. The loop gain 2 is not the sensitivity.

retired_questions.prompt: Same loop. The closed-loop gain is
retired_questions.explanation: \(T = G/(1+L) = 10/(1+2) = 10/3 = 3.333\). The loop gain 2 is not the closed-loop gain. Adding 1 to \(G\) instead of to \(L\) gives \(10/11\), which is wrong.

retired_questions.prompt: The complementary sensitivity \(T(s)\) and the sensitivity \(S(s)\) satisfy
retired_questions.explanation: \(T = L/(1+L)\) and \(S = 1/(1+L)\). Their sum is \((L+1)/(1+L) = 1\). Zero is wrong because both \(T\) and \(S\) are positive. Their product is \(L/(1+L)^2\), not 1. Their difference is \((L-1)/(1+L)\), not \(L\).

retired_questions.prompt: On a Nyquist plot, the loop gain \(L(j\omega)\) is plotted as \(\omega\) sweeps from 0 to \(\infty\). The critical point is at
retired_questions.explanation: Stability depends on encirclements of \(-1\), the point where \(1 + L = 0\). The origin is where \(L = 0\), not the critical point. The point \(+1\) is where \(L = 1\), which is not the instability boundary. The point \(j\) is on the imaginary axis and is not special for stability.

retired_questions.prompt: Robust performance requires that the loop gain satisfy constraints on
retired_questions.explanation: Robust performance bounds depend on how \(L(j\omega)\) moves in the complex plane. That requires magnitude and phase at every frequency. The DC gain alone is a single point. The forward or return alone is not the loop product.
